solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pop padding novel summary with many, many pages

indicators.note: padding stuffs material into something, so one piece is packed inside the other

parts.note: a coda is the concluding section that rounds off a novel or piece of music
a ream is about 500 sheets of paper, so reams are a vast number of pages

explanation.surface: A publisher bulks out a short synopsis of a novel with page after page of filler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like a verb or a father, but it is the fizzy drink. 'Summary' is loose for a coda, which rounds a story off; the filler goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop is an informal word for a fizzy soft drink, and cream soda is one vanilla-flavoured kind.

clue.text: 100 years — not half clever age

indicators.note: not half means only half is kept, so the back half of the word is dropped

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
Y is the standard abbreviation for year
a deletion: the first half of the six-letter word, three letters

explanation.surface: Someone lives a hundred years and is only half as sharp in old age.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes '100 years' look like a century being defined, but the definition is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cycle can mean a very long period or era, the same loose sense as an age in history.

clue.text: Husband withdrawing from torment — no time for such pain!

indicators.note: withdrawing from something means leaving it, so this letter is taken out
no here means without, so the following letter is removed as well

parts.note: heartache is emotional torment
T is the abbreviation for time
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A tormented husband walks out, with no time for all the grief.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the H and the T out of HEARTACHE to leave EARACHE. 'Such pain' points back to the torment theme while defining a physical ache.
explanation.definitionFit: Earache is a common physical pain felt inside the ear, so it is one kind of pain.

clue.text: Spiteful mother fast to trap rodent

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: trapping something shuts it inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
a vole is a small rodent

explanation.surface: A nasty mother moves quickly to catch a rat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' reads as quick, but it is the noun, a period of abstinence: LENT, which holds the rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: Malevolent means wishing harm on others, a close synonym of spiteful.

clue.text: Group company backing New Year festival

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
Tet is the Vietnamese lunar New Year festival

explanation.surface: A firm sponsors a New Year celebration for a group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads as sponsoring, but it turns the company abbreviation round. Tet is the Vietnamese New Year, a festival crossword setters use often.
explanation.definitionFit: An octet is a set of eight performers or things, so it is a particular kind of group.

clue.text: Saudis note paper made totally unrestricted recordings here

indicators.note: without restriction at either end, each word loses its boundary letters on both sides

parts.note: the inner four letters
the inner two letters
the inner three letters

explanation.surface: Saudi officials note that a newspaper published recordings without any censorship.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of 'Saudis note paper' is stripped of its first and last letters. The definition is descriptive: the tape is where the recordings are made.
explanation.definitionFit: Audiotape is magnetic tape on which sound is recorded, so recordings are held on it.

clue.text: Unearth little dog I had briefly rejected

indicators.note: briefly means in short form, so the phrase is cut down to its abbreviation
something rejected is sent back, so the letters are returned in reverse order

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone digs out a small dog they owned for a short while and then gave up.
explanation.walkthrough: The contraction I'D loses its apostrophe; the whole string PUGID is then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig up is to bring something out of the ground by excavating, the literal sense of unearth.

clue.text: Crudely paint bishop, covered by diamonds and gold

indicators.note: in a down entry, being covered by means sitting underneath, so this letter comes last

parts.note: D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A garish portrait of a bishop smothered in jewels and gold leaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Because this is a down clue, the bishop sits beneath the diamonds and gold.
explanation.definitionFit: To daub is to smear paint on roughly and carelessly, without skill.

clue.text: Creole stew almost evil — it stings my mouth

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: gumbo is a thick Creole stew from Louisiana
ill, meaning evil or harm, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A diner complains that a spicy Creole stew burns the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the stew burning the mouth; the definition is the whole last phrase. ILL as a noun means evil, as in 'speak no ill'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gumboil is a painful abscess on the gum, so it is something that hurts inside the mouth.

clue.text: A native fed Timmy peeled fruit

indicators.note: being fed means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a native is a person born in a place

indicators.note: peeling removes the skin, so the outermost letters are stripped away

parts.note: the name without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A local feeds little Timmy some fruit with the skin taken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peeled' sounds like it describes the fruit, but it strips the boy's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The persimmon is an orange tomato-like fruit from a tree of the ebony family.

clue.text: Before end of night, left wearing charmer's ring

indicators.note: whoever is worn is draped around the wearer, so the wearer sits inside

parts.note: Circe is the enchantress of the Odyssey who charmed men into pigs
L is the abbreviation for left

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: A seducer left before the night ended, still wearing her ring.
explanation.walkthrough: CIRCE wraps round L, and the whole comes before the T. Circe is the witch of Greek myth who bewitched Odysseus's crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A circlet is a small circular band or ornament, often worn on the head or finger, so a ring.

clue.text: Band member departs with stranger

parts.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
rummer here is the comparative of rum, meaning odd

explanation.surface: A musician walks out of the group with a newcomer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stranger' is not a person but the adjective 'more strange'; rum is British slang for odd, so rummer means stranger.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer plays percussion and is a standard member of a rock or marching band.

clue.text: Dig European bubbly, cracking processed toxin!

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: cracking something means breaking into it, so one piece goes inside another
something processed has been broken down and reworked, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
cava is a Spanish sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A jibe at a European sparkling wine that has been adulterated with poison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dig' looks like a verb or a jibe, but it is the noun for an archaeological site. CAVA breaks into the rearranged letters after the X.
explanation.definitionFit: An excavation is an archaeological dig, the site where earth is removed to uncover remains.

clue.text: Greeting US soldier who can get into advanced positions

definitions.text: who can get into advanced positions

parts.note: yo is a casual American greeting
GI is the term for an American soldier

explanation.surface: A salute for the American soldier who can push forward into forward military positions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced positions' sounds military, fitting the soldier, but it means difficult yoga postures.
explanation.definitionFit: A yogi is a practitioner of yoga, able to hold demanding bodily postures once trained.

clue.text: Censured commercial — gross hedonism!

parts.note: an ad is a commercial, an advertisement

indicators.note: gross means coarse or crude, suggesting the letters are roughly mangled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A television advert is condemned for promoting disgusting self-indulgence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' looks like an adjective of disapproval describing the hedonism, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: To admonish is to reprimand firmly, so admonished and censured are synonyms in the past tense.

clue.text: Abide with hollow surrounds

indicators.note: to surround is to enclose on all sides, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded hollow or valley
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: An old hymn-like phrase about staying put in a sheltered valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abide with' echoes the hymn 'Abide with Me', but 'with' belongs to the wordplay as W.
explanation.definitionFit: Both abide and dwell mean to live or remain in a place, an old-fashioned synonym pair.

clue.text: Denigrate quality of feathers?

parts.note: down is the soft fine feathers of birds
a grade is a level of quality

explanation.surface: A snide remark about how good some feathers are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quality of feathers' is read as the grade of down, so the pieces are put in the opposite order to the clue. The question mark flags the playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To downgrade something is to lower its status or belittle it, close to denigrating it.

clue.text: Old nan collects first impressions of Stieg Larsson, all this year's titles

indicators.note: collecting something gathers it in, so one piece is taken inside the other

parts.note: grandam is an archaic word for grandmother

indicators.note: a first impression is the opening glimpse, so only initial letters are kept

parts.note: the initial of each name

explanation.surface: A grandmother gathers her opinions on the Swedish crime novelist's books, and every new release this year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' belongs with 'nan' to give the archaic word. A nan is a British name for a grandmother.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand slam is winning every major championship in a sport within one season, such as tennis or rugby.

clue.text: Good boy, Italy's No 1 player, caught out fierce campaigner

indicators.note: out means removed or dismissed, so this letter is taken away

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a lad is a boy

indicators.note: number one is the first in line, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter
a player is an actor on stage
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A good lad becomes Italy's top sportsman but is dismissed, caught, in a fierce contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught out' looks like a cricket dismissal, but it means remove C from ACTOR. In cricket scoring c stands for caught.
explanation.definitionFit: A gladiator figuratively means someone who fights hard for a cause, a combative public champion.

clue.text: Northern Counties Division fans at new peak

indicators.note: to fan is to spread out and scatter, so the letters are dispersed and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Supporters of a northern football league team celebrate reaching a new high.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a football league with supporters; 'fans' is actually the verb. 'New' is part of the letters, not a second signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A wapentake was an old administrative subdivision of Yorkshire and other northern and Midland English shires.

clue.text: After draining Pilsener, former PM cut short waffling speech

indicators.note: cut short means clipped at the end, so the last letter is lost
draining empties out the contents, so only the outer shell of letters remains

parts.note: its first and last letters
Clement Attlee, Labour Prime Minister 1945 to 1951, missing his final letter

explanation.surface: After downing a lager, an old prime minister cuts his rambling speech short.
explanation.walkthrough: Attlee was the British Labour Prime Minister after the Second World War. Pilsener is a pale lager.
explanation.definitionFit: Prattle is foolish, inconsequential talk that goes on at length, much like waffle.

clue.text: Voided O-level study from former times

indicators.note: something voided has been emptied of its contents, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: its first and last letters
a den is a private study room

explanation.surface: Studying for an O-level, a school exam that has since been abolished, belongs to the past.
explanation.walkthrough: O-levels were British school exams for sixteen-year-olds, replaced in 1988.
explanation.definitionFit: Olden is an old-fashioned adjective meaning belonging to the distant past, as in the olden days.

clue.text: Random drunk clasping old security guard

indicators.note: clasping holds something tight within, so one piece is gripped inside
someone drunk staggers about unsteadily, so these letters lurch into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An arbitrary drunk grabs an elderly man guarding the door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Random drunk' reads as a stranger who is drunk; 'random' is the letters and 'drunk' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorman stands at the entrance of a club or building, controlling who enters, like a bouncer.

clue.text: Mutt runs around carrying a pointy stick

indicators.note: running around means turning back the other way, so the letters face the opposite direction
carrying something holds it within, so one piece is borne inside

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog dashes about with a sharp stick in its mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs around' seems to describe the dog chasing about, but it turns the dog backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A goad is a spiked rod used to prod cattle forward, literally a pointed stick.

clue.text: Jim, is Eric or Dave garnering support in the church?

indicators.note: garnering means gathering in and storing, so the letters sit gathered within the words

parts.note: runs from the end of the first name to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A question about which of three men is winning backing from the congregation.
explanation.walkthrough: The three names look like candidates seeking support, but they only carry the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A misericord is a ledge under a hinged choir-stall seat, giving standing clergy something to lean on.

clue.text: Cut up manuscript papers

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to axe is to cut
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: Someone shreds handwritten documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut up' reads as a single verb for shredding, but 'up' only turns 'cut' backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Exam papers are the sheets of questions sat in a test, so exams are called papers.

clue.text: Italian magistrate eating last bit of roasted duck

indicators.note: eating takes food inside, so one piece is swallowed within the other

parts.note: the doge was the chief magistrate of Venice or Genoa

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: A Venetian official dines on roast duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' sits in the scene as the dish, but it is the verb meaning to avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck and to dodge both mean to avoid something by moving quickly aside.

clue.text: Huge barrel containing sulphur

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: a vat is a large tank or cask
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: An enormous cask full of sulphur.
explanation.walkthrough: S is the chemical symbol for sulphur, a convention setters lean on constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Vast and huge are synonyms, both describing something of immense size or extent.

clue.text: Pull a wagon back, laden with tons and tons

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back means in the opposite direction, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for ton

indicators.note: something laden carries a load, and here the load wraps around it

parts.note: a cart is a wagon
T again, for the second ton

explanation.surface: A horse hauls a wagon backwards, heavily loaded with many tons.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the wagon carrying the load; in the wordplay the two Ts hold the reversed wagon between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To attract is to draw something towards you, as a magnet does, so it means to pull.

clue.text: Red-faced individual responsible for fake news?

parts.note: a means one, a single individual
a sham is a fake
ED is short for editor, the person responsible for the news

explanation.surface: An embarrassed journalist blamed for spreading disinformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fake news' reads as one phrase, but the wordplay splits it: a sham editor. The question mark flags the playful parse.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ashamed is embarrassed by guilt and blushes, so their face goes red.

clue.text: Leave former partner, retiring in Scotland too

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the letters go into reverse

parts.note: tae is the Scots form of too

explanation.surface: Someone walks out on an ex who is also withdrawing in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a verb, but it is the noun: permission to be absent. An exeat is leave from a British boarding school or college.
explanation.definitionFit: An exeat is formal permission for temporary absence, granted by a school or college, so leave.

clue.text: Possibly Villa, maybe Reading — English team knocked out regularly

parts.note: reading is one of the three Rs of basic education
E is the abbreviation for English
a side is a sports team

indicators.note: taking letters out at regular intervals leaves every other letter standing

parts.note: its second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A football report: Aston Villa and Reading both see an English side eliminated.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa and Reading are English football clubs, but here a villa is a house and Reading is one of the three Rs.
explanation.definitionFit: A villa is a kind of house, and a residence is any home, so a villa is an example.
